### 2026-10-22 – # KeySync - Day 1

**3h**

# KeySync - Day 1
### Project planning and initial schematic

Today, I started planning my new hardware project, KeySync, a custom MIDI keyboard designed to combine music tech, electronics and pcb design. My goal is to make a compact personalized MIDI controller that can interact with music production software but also lets me build a more advanced circuit board.

For the main microcontroller, I decieded to use the XIAO ESP32-C3 because it's cheaper and I'm broke. This microcontroller will process the inputs and communicate with a computer. However, the xiao is limited in its ports so the controller will only feature capacitive touch switches, low profile switches and a rotary encoder.

My first focus was to identify the components I would need before beginning the schematic in KiCad. I  started by downloading the necessary footprints and symbol libraries before configuring them as well as the symbol pathways.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/564384879cdefb04f8d96ada0d2a8e9e859f740253240045990b234e9fb9753a.png)

From there I began importing my parts into the schematic. I started with the capacitive keys that I'm going to use a 01x07 switch. I needed to research and check online for the correct pin layout that would allow the xiao to actually read the inputs so I connected the switches 7 pins to d0-d5 and d10.

Next were the two low profile switches which I connected to ground together and wired to Xiao's d6 and d7 pins. After I wired up the rotary encoder by connecting its A and B ports to D8 and D9 while connection the MB and C ports to ground. I cut off the S1 and S2 ports. On top of this I also added the ground, 3.3v and 5v connection for the XIAO, completing the schematic

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/1c42d321533c459851d670522f2b695c06cbafdf064cf0ec88ae7ae6ff1793c8.png)

Finally, I assigned the footprints to every component that I had downloaded from before and saved the footprints tags to my schematic. The switches (SW_PUSH) were just assigned to the "Kailh Choc Low-Profile Switches" footprint I downloaded, while the rotary encoder was assigned the vertical EC11 footprint. For now I left the 01x07 switch footprint empty to customize it's footprint as a capitative keys later.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/43f9750ba8a121c98feb28181f2d089e4ca62cb5e244f5f370d0cf1ba0dcabba.png)

Summary: Finished up my project design and connected all the different components in the schematic as well as assigning their footprints which had to be downloaded.

Next time: Begin designing the actual PCB and adding custom details.

### 2026-10-25 – # KeySync — Day 2: Custom Footprints, PCB Layout, A lot of Revisions and Routing

**6h**

# KeySync — Day 2: Custom Footprints, PCB Layout, A lot of Revisions and Routing
Oct 23th, 2026 + Oct 24th

Today, I focused on building the physical PCB design for KeySync from the completed schematic. My goal was to create the custom copper electrodes for the capacitive touch keys, establish the board outline, position the components, and complete the routing.

## 1. Designing Custom Heart-Shaped Touch Pads

One of my first tasks was building the custom footprint for the capacitive touch keys. When thinking about what custom shape I wanted to use for the pads, I decided I wanted them to have a heart shape from the game UNDERTALE. I thought it would be a perfect fit since one of my favourite game soundtracks is UNDERTALE and one of the most prominent images is the 7 souls so I could have each pad represent a soul.

I created the heart-shaped pads in KiCad, sketching out a polygon based on a reference image before merging it with a pad. Then I copied it and arranged all 7 hearts like how they show up in the game.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/3cb803fb7cc51d2ebe8a8520a3d273fe268216d396b77e4dded359b6b76fb81f.png)

From there I built a rectangular courtyard around my pads on the F.courtyard layer. Before saving my footprint, adding it to a custom library and assigning it to the component in my schematic.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/f3fae04b80e63f3232d394e5d5eda3e167df030cfd3a075de30c27c069763c64.png)

## 2. Building the Physical PCB and Board Outline

After designing the touch pads, I began turning the schematic into a physical PCB layout. I imported the XIAO ESP32, low-profile switches, rotary encoder, and my new footprint for the touch keys while thinking about how their connections would be routed.

I created the PCB board outline to establish the board's physical boundaries. Originally, I planned on having a heart shaped PCB outline like this image. But then I realized that it would look bad since my keys were already heart shaped so I decided to go with a simple rectangular outline. This gave me a clear reference for my components and helped me assess how much space was available for the complete design.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/f33a7bcc1439260dd059f8836248ace7c0c061abe935710c7b758a4c0a9f3012.png)

## 3. Fixing the capacitive key Footprint
One problem I ran into was that the capacitive key footprint was too big for the actual PCB layout, first I tried just shrinking the courtyard, then I tried bringing the pads closer before realizing that the hearts were too big so I redid my footprint. I reimported my reference image, scaled it down, recopied the hearts and merged them with pads to finish up my new properly sized footprint. This taught me that I can't just assume a footprint will fit because it looks fine in KiCad. I need to check its dimensions and make sure it matches the actual component I'm planning to use.

From there, I reimported all my components from the schematic onto my PCB and organized them but quickly realized I had another small issue.

## 4. Fixing the schematic

When I was organizing what components I wanted where on my board, I decided I wanted the two switches to be on one side of the microcontroller with the encoder on the left side and the keys below everything. But then as I started routing I realized that my encoder had a lot of connection on the right side of the esp32 so I went into my schematic to redo all my connections.

I moved two of the key connections to the right side to move the encoder connections to the left, this way the encoder and switches were able to easily be routed to the esp32. I imported my components into the PCB  again and arranged them again this time checking the routes to make sure I could easily route all my components.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/5be3b5ce95772a9fb5f19a9c5687262debaed7e6bd820f6657db7a4047e0429f.png)

As I worked on the PCB, I noticed that I needed to make some changes to the schematic and how certain components were connected. I also had to change the pad numbers on some of my custom footprints a few times to make routing easier.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/c5e709598448d15a3f29f21666e9c2e65f1013f27e32c75e582e49acedcf6f73.png)

Here you can see a picture of my edited schematic where I moved the components to where they would physically be on the board while also redoing some of the connections.

## 5. Routing the Pad numbers
I began routing everything but realized my pad numbers and their respective connections on the esp32 were all over the place. Originally I had numbered my pads left to right going down but I realized that this method meant I would block off some of the connections.

From there I did some quick trial and error where instead of changing the schematic, I changed the pad numbers, imported the new version of the footprint and checked how they routed.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/db9d789be0d4675b0c3e20654bf21aaad7d57af6f4e3a4749e5e710d8f28d548.png)
Picture of one of my edits which wasn't even the final version.

But after a bit of time, I ended with a layout that I thought routed easily enough to use.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/d861cf255de37acf50f962866cb84b73c70e1f7dda8d35bbeaa93a17f53c39a2.png)

## 6. Routing the components
So now that all my components could be routed easily, I decided to do my keys on the F.cu layer and the other switches + encoder on the B.cu layer which ultimately gave me this.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/EgY3s8kanBhx0FNjeHxRsejCAPHT6ftU/9668946ea7cc0dc21e1f5ebc9090da37b89cf93090e83c221d0db8b212c5862a.png)

## Summary

I created seven heart-shaped touch pads, finished the board outline, fixed an oversized footprint, and made changes to the schematic and pad numbers. I also finished routing the switches on the back copper layer and the touch keys on the front. Most of the main PCB layout is now done, so I can start focusing on the artwork and checking that everything is ready to be manufactured.

## Next steps
- Add extra UNDERTALE/DELTARUNE-inspired art and the KeySync name as well as my initials into the PCB silkscreen.
- Check the 3D view to make sure the components fit and there are no obvious spacing issues.
- Put together a bill of materials (BOM) listing the parts I'll need.
- Start properly building  the GitHub README with the project description, components, design process, and progress pictures.
